https://www.politico.eu/article/what-ice.text: BRUSSELS — For years, Brussels has sold EU membership as a shield against an unpredictable world: safety, stability and strength in numbers. With Russia’s war in Ukraine raging and Donald Trump upending the global order — and going so far as threatening to invade Greenland — the EU hoped it had been cast in a more appealing light, despite the challenges caused by the rise of the far right, crises on its doorstep, and trade disputes with the U.S. and China. Iceland’s vote not to reopen membership talks has shown that’s not necessarily the case. Advertisement Advertisement “At a time when the international security environment has become far more uncertain than it was a decade ago, many expected support for reopening accession negotiations to grow,” said Nicola Procaccini, co-chair of the right-wing European Conservatives and Reformists group in the European Parliament. “The fact that the Icelandic people nevertheless chose not to take even that first step should give Brussels pause.” Reykjavik’s narrow rejection of restarting EU accession talks in a referendum on Saturday is hardly a death blow to the 450 million-strong bloc. With fewer than 400,000 people and a smaller GDP than Estonia, Iceland was never the prize that would make or break Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s European project. But the result is still an uncomfortable reality check for a Brussels establishment that has spent the past four years betting that a hazardous world would make the EU more attractive — and had taken Iceland’s renewed interest as a flattering signal of its own relevance. “A nation weighed what membership would add to what it already has,” center-right Finnish MEP Mika Aaltola said, “and answered: not enough.” Vote of (no) confidence Enlargement is about more than adding countries to the EU. It is also a branding exercise: a way for Brussels to show that its model of democracy, prosperity and predictability remains attractive in a world of hard power politics. Every country that knocks on the EU’s door gives the bloc a chance to present itself as a desirable club, in contrast to Trump’s claims that the continent is “decaying.” Iceland was unusually useful in that regard: a wealthy democracy that paused its membership bid in 2015, but was coming back and asking to be let in. Advertisement Advertisement In the run-up to Reykjavík’s referendum, the bloc’s enlargement chief, Marta Kos, overtly framed it as a vote of confidence in the EU. “It would confirm our growing attractiveness in a world that is rapidly changing,” she told POLITICO. The result of the referendum, then, would appear to signal the opposite. “Iceland was demotivating,” said an EU official who, like others in this story, was granted anonymity to speak freely. “Even a frozen country doesn’t want to be a part of the EU.” The response from the European Commission has, so far, been a disappointed shrug. A Commission spokesperson gave a clipped statement, saying it “takes note” of the result and would remain a “close partner” of Iceland. But a diplomat from a candidate country was gloomier, calling the result a huge blow to the bloc’s enlargement ambitions and the EU’s image more generally. Far-right, Euroskeptic leaders — from Marine Le Pen to Nigel Farage — immediately seized on the referendum’s failure, that diplomat pointed out, making the case for enlargement that much harder. Reykjavik’s return to the negotiating table could have added momentum to the candidacies of Moldova, Ukraine and Albania, all of which are looking to advance their own paths toward membership. And Montenegro, which has closed over half its accession chapters, was eager to join the bloc at the same time as Iceland to help get its bid ratified. Advertisement Advertisement A second diplomat from a different candidate country was more optimistic about the consequences of Iceland’s negative vote, however. While their first reaction was disappointment, that diplomat said they expected Brussels would focus even more on getting the advanced candidate countries that are eager to join, especially Montenegro, over the line. Security nothingburger For Icelandic voters, the reasons for saying No boiled down to a few key issues: fishing rights, sovereignty, the economy, and the fact that Iceland is already inside the European Economic Area and Schengen Area, getting many of the benefits of being in the EU without having to bear the full cost of membership. Yet the biggest draw was supposed to be security. With Trump looming over Greenland, and using trade to coerce allies and enemies alike, safety in numbers inside the bloc suddenly seemed like an appealing prospect for tiny, remote Iceland. “We are living in a completely different world than just 10 years ago,” Icelandic Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir, who hails from a pro-EU party, told POLITICO before the vote. Ahead of the referendum, a Commission official said Trump had done the bloc a favor. Yet Saturday’s referendum shows that while the EU’s promise of solidarity remains compelling for poorer, post-communist states on the bloc’s eastern flank, such as Moldova, Montenegro and Ukraine, security alone is not enough to lure richer, already well-integrated countries like Iceland, but also Norway and Switzerland, into the club. Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson, Iceland’s longest-serving president and an opponent of EU membership, said the Trump fear factor was just not a convincing enough argument, given that Iceland is a founding member of NATO and has a long-standing bilateral security agreement with the U.S. “There’s no shred of evidence that President Trump’s administration has any intention whatsoever in weakening that agreement,” he argued. Advertisement Advertisement “We spent 100 years in a struggle against the Danish king and the Danish authorities in order to gain full independence,” Grímsson added, arguing Icelanders were loath to “start sharing that sovereignty in one way or another.” Gabriel Gavin and Max Griera contributed to this report. https://www.dw.com/en/spain-s-parliament.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NfTv Parliamentarians voted with a crowd of protesters outside awaiting the results Image: Manu Fernandez/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Spain 's parliament has narrowly voted down a pair of emergency government decrees aiming to quell widespread protests against rising rental costs for housing. Hundreds of protesters were gathered outside the parliament in Madrid amid the marathon debate culminating in a pair of votes on Friday. They yelled "shame" and "your profits, our misery," as news of the measures being quashed filtered through. Spain has been gripped by protests for around a week , including a tent city set up in central Madrid, ignited by the eviction of an 87-year-old pensioner from her apartment that threw the more longstanding issue of unaffordable housing costs into sharp focus. Why and how did the emergency decrees fail? Left-leaning Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez leads a minority government in Spain and so relies on opposition support to legislate. Sanchez spoke at the close of a marathon 5-hour debate in the Chamber of Deputies ahead of the vote, urging members: "Do the right thing, or history will judge you, and sooner than you think." Sanchez tried to rally majority support for the measures at the last in parliament, but could not succeed Image: Eduardo Parra/Europa Press/AP Photo/picture alliance One Catalan party that sometimes supports Sanchez's government, the economically right-leaning Junts group, joined the opposition in voting down the measures. The first emergency decree, which the government said would stop evictions of vulnerable people, make real estate speculation harder and provide tax incentives to encourage renting, failed by a narrow margin of 178-172. The second decree, which sought to make residential leases automatically renewable by tenants, fell further short of a majority at 184-166. Opponents to the measures argued, among other things, that they risked compounding the situation by reducing housing supply. Some also argued that Sanchez should respond to the deadlock by calling early elections, possibly initiating a wholesale change of government. Rising rents were a sensitive issue in Spain for years, but one particularly emotive eviction brought it to the boil Image: Manu Fernandez/AP Photo/picture alliance What did protesters say after the vote? The Tenants' Union which had led protests across Spain said it would press on with plans for more mass rallies on Saturday, aiming to continue heaping pressure on the coalition and opposition alike. "The encampment will continue and will continue expanding to other neighborhoods," Tenants' Union spokesperson Alicia del Rio said. "We're aiming for a general strike." The current wave of protests, albeit concerning an issue that's been bubbling away near the surface for years, was triggered by the high-profile eviction of 87-year-old Madrid resident Maricarmen Abascal from the apartment she had occupied for almost all of her life. Maricarmen Abascal has since been granted a reprieve, but the more widespread attempts to improve the situation remain stalled for now Image: Francesco Militello Mirto/IPA/ZUMA/picture alliance How tough is Spain's housing market? The investment company owning Abascal's building reversed the measure in her case this week but only after the issue had become a symbol of growing frustration of housing costs. Rents have roughly doubled in Spain in the last decade and young people, facing one of Europe's toughest labor markets for school-leavers and graduates, frequently live with their parents past the age of 30. "People have said 'enough is enough;' this ⁠cannot ​go on. The housing problem must be resolved; structural measures must be taken, and this cannot ​continue," Abascal's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, said in an interview with Reuters on Thursday. The next step after Friday's failed vote in parliament is difficult to identify. Sanchez has so far ruled out calling early elections. He could try to formulate another emergency decree or decrees in response to the protests, but any such move would need to overcome the same hurdles in parliament. Photograph: Mitchell Layton/Getty Images US policing Discovery of North Carolina police officers’ alleged racist texts prompts review of arrest records ‘Deeply troubling’ messages came to light during investigation into misuse of Flock camera system Richard Luscombe Tue 20 Oct 2026 09.28 EDT Last modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 09.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Five officers resigned recently from a North Carolina police agency – and a sixth remained suspended – after they allegedly exchanged racist texts. The chief of the Charlotte-Mecklenburg police department (CMPD) said the messages came to light during an investigation into misuse of its Flock camera system. The department on Monday released personnel files identifying the officers after a public information request by local media. The discovery of the “deeply troubling” messages, said Estella Patterson, the police chief, at a news conference on Thursday, prompted a full review of body-worn camera footage and arrest records of the officers – and a request to the FBI for a civil rights investigation. “As a Black woman who began my career here in this very department, it is especially painful and disheartening to hear concerns from our community about racism coming from within the ranks of this organization,” Patterson said. “Although the officers involved in this investigation were hired before my tenure as chief, that does not lessen my responsibility or my commitment to making sure that what was discovered in this case is not a systemic problem in this organization.” Patterson did not disclose the content of the texts, which contained racist slurs and alleged use of the N-word, according to ABC News . The five former officers were named by the CMPD on Monday as Mateo Juarez, Joseph Kelly, Tredan Maronic, Matthew Osborn and Alexander Larsen. All were hired in 2023 or 2024, and Patterson had cited them for termination. According to Charlotte news outlet WSOC , one was president of their recruit class, and another received an employee of the month award earlier in the year. The outlet said one of the messages likened the officers to a “clan rally”, an apparent reference to rallies held by the murderous white nationalist Ku Klux Klan . A sixth officer, Jeremiah Todman, who was hired in 2022, remains suspended pending the outcome of the investigation and a civil service board review, the CMPD said in a statement. A seventh officer, Seth Elliot, resigned in August after being alleged to have improperly viewed Flock camera data. Elliot’s resignation came days after his arrest by the North Carolina Bureau of Investigation for illegally accessing a government computer. “The department remains committed to accountability and providing access to public records in accordance with the law, while respecting the integrity of any ongoing investigations and potential legal proceedings,” the CMPD statement said. So far, none of the officers have been charged with any criminal wrongdoing in relation to the text exchanges. ABC said it was unclear if any of them other than Elliott had retained an attorney – and reported that his lawyer, George Laughrun, did not return a request for comment. The Guardian has contacted the Charlotte-Mecklenburg Fraternal Order of Police lodge that represents the department’s officers for comment. Beside pursuing the officers’ termination, Patterson said she intended to seek the revocation of their state law licenses. She said the episode had prompted her to review how the CMPD interacts with the public. “I have been concerned whether this type of behavior is systemic throughout the department,” she said. “We have begun and will continue auditing [body-worn camera] footage. We’re going to look at the interactions that our officers are having with members of the public to make sure that they are outstanding. “The overwhelming majority of our employees do exceptional work every single day. They come to work to serve this community, and they demonstrate that in their actions. They do their work with respect, with compassion, and professionalism. “We will not allow the misconduct of a few to define the whole.” Explore more on these topics US policing Charlotte North Carolina Race news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
